title: TOP 10 Deepest Caves on Earth Even Scientists Were Afraid to Map
fullText: In 2018, a team of Russian cave explorers descended into a hole in the mountains of the western Caucasus. They climbed down for 5 days. They set up underground camps at depths where no sunlight has reached in millions of years. They squeezed through passages so narrow that they had to exhale completely to fit their rib cages through the rock. At 2,212 m below the surface, deeper than six Empire State buildings stacked on top of each other, they found a river. It was flowing. They could hear it in the darkness before they saw it. Nobody knows where it goes. In another cave in the Mexican desert, crystals taller than a fourstory building grow in a chamber where the air temperature is 58° C and the humidity is 99%. A human being without protective equipment loses consciousness in roughly 10 minutes. In a cave beneath New Mexico, scientists discovered bacteria living in total darkness on bare rock. Bacteria that had never been exposed to antibiotics in their entire evolutionary history. When researchers tested them, the bacteria were already resistant to drugs that humans had not invented yet. And in Ecuador in 1976, Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on the moon, descended into a cave in the jungle. Not for geology, not for tourism. He went because someone told him there was a library hidden underground. A library made of metal built by a civilization that no historian has ever been able to identify. These are not metaphors. These are real places. This is our countdown of the 10 deepest, most extreme caves on Earth that even scientists were afraid to map. Stay until the end because number one is that cave in the Caucasus and what the team found at the bottom has never been explained. Before we start, drop a comment telling us where you are watching from right now. We want to see how many countries this video reaches. Number 10, Icevelt, Verin, Salsburg, Austria. Inside the Hulkal Mountain in the Austrian Alps, roughly 40 kilometers south of Salsburg, there is a cave system that stretches over 42 kilometers into the rock. The first kilometer is made of ice. Not frozen water dripping from a ceiling. Entire chambers filled with ice formations. Walls of blue white ice reaching from floor to ceiling. Frozen waterfalls suspended mid cascade. Ice columns thicker than tree trunks standing in caverns large enough to hold a cathedral. According to the Austrian Federal Geological Survey, the ice reason is the largest ice cave in the world by volume of ice contained. The cave was discovered in 1879 by Anton Posult, an Austrian naturalist. According to records preserved by the Salsburg Museum, Poselt entered roughly 200 m before the cold and darkness forced him to turn back. He published his findings. Nobody cared. The cave was ignored for over 40 years. In 1912, Alexander von Mor, a speliologist from Salsburg, organized the first deep exploration. His team pushed pastel's limit and discovered the ice palace beyond chambers with names like the ice gate, the hemier hall, and the great ice wall. Von Mor mapped over a kilometer of ice passages. According to his expedition notes preserved by the Austrian Alpine Club, the temperature inside the ice section remains at or below zero year round, even during summer when the outside temperature exceeds 25°. The ice exists because of air flow. According to glaciological studies published by the University of Insbrook, the ice reason functions as a cold air trap. In winter, cold air flows into the cave's lower entrance and freezes any water present. In summer, the warmer air cannot displace the dense cold air already trapped inside. The ice accumulates over centuries and never fully melts. But here is what makes the cave unsettling. Beyond the ice section, past the frozen waterfalls in the blue walls, the cave continues for another 41 km. The rock passages beyond the ice are not frozen. They are dark, dry, and largely unexplored. According to the Austrian Speliological Society, less than a quarter of the total system has been fully surveyed. Alexander von Mort never saw the exploration completed. He was killed in World War I in 1914, 2 years after his discovery. His ashes were placed inside the cave in the ice section he mapped. They are still there in an urn on a natural shelf of rock surrounded by ice that has been forming since before his grandparents were born. 42 km of darkness inside a mountain. The first kilometer made of ice that has been building for centuries. The other 41 km unmapped, unlit and waiting. Number nine, Soteno de lasolandrinas, San Luis Potosi, Mexico. In the mountains of the Sierra Madre Oriental in central Mexico, there is a hole in the ground that drops 370 m straight down. No slope, no staircase, no gradual descent. a vertical shaft open to the sky at the top, narrowing slightly, then widening into a chamber at the bottom large enough to fit the Chrysler building. According to measurements published by the Association for Mexican Cave Studies, the main shaft of Sautano de Lasandrinas is roughly 60 m wide at the surface and expands to approximately 300 m wide at the base. The freef fall distance from the lip to the floor is 370 m, roughly 1,214 ft. It is one of the deepest vertical cave shafts on Earth. The cave was first explored by modern speliologists in 1966. According to expedition records from the Association for Mexican Cave Studies, the team lowered a weighted rope into the shaft and waited. The rope took over 7 seconds to reach the bottom. The sound of the weight hitting the floor took another second to travel back up. The name means basement of the swallows, but the birds that inhabit the cave are not swallows. They are white collared swifts and green parakeetses. According to ornithological surveys conducted by the Universad Autonom San Luis Potosi, tens of thousands of birds roost on the walls of the shaft. Every morning at dawn they leave. The exit is not a casual departure. The birds cannot simply fly out. The shaft is too deep and too narrow for a direct vertical ascent from the bottom. Instead, they spiral. Thousands of birds rotating in a counterclockwise helix inside the shaft, rising in a column of beating wings that take several minutes to clear the opening. The sound echoes off the limestone walls, a roar that people standing at the rim describe as unlike anything they have heard elsewhere. At dusk, the birds return. They fold their wings and dive. They enter the shaft at the top and freef fall into the darkness, opening their wings at the last moment to break before hitting the walls. Researchers have measured their descent speeds at over 100 km hour. base jumpers have leapt into the shaft. The freef fall lasts roughly 10 seconds. According to accounts published in climbing and adventure sports journals, jumpers describe the experience as falling into the earth itself, the walls closing in, the light shrinking to a circle above, the floor invisible until the parachute opens. A hole in the ground that drops the height of a skyscraper. Tens of thousands of birds spiraling out at dawn and diving back in at dusk and a floor that sits in permanent twilight receiving a few minutes of direct sunlight per day when the angle is exactly right then returning to shadow. Number eight, Hong Va Fong Na Kbang, Vietnam. In the limestone carsted mountains of central Vietnam, roughly 50 kilometers from the border with Laos, a cave was discovered in 2012 that contains something no speliologist had seen before. Inside the main chamber of Hongva, the floor is covered in terrace pools of calsite. Hundreds of them stepping down in concentric tears. Each pool filled with still minerals saturated water. The formations look like flooded rice patties carved into stone. The resemblance is so precise that the first expedition photographs were initially questioned as digitally altered. According to survey data published by the British Cave Research Association, which co-led the exploration with the Vietnam National University of Science, Hong Va is part of the Fong Na Kang cave system, one of the largest karst networks in Asia. The cave itself extends roughly 1.7 km, but the calsight terrace chamber is what sets it apart from every other cave on Earth. The terraces are formed by a process called rimstone damning. According to geochemical analysis published by the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology, minerals saturated water seeps into the cave through the limestone ceiling and flows across the cave floor. As the water loses carbon dioxide to the cave atmosphere, dissolved calcium carbonate precipitates out and solidifies at the water's edge, building thin dams of calite that trap the water behind them. Over thousands of years, the dams grow taller, the pools deepen, and the floor transforms into a staircase of still water. The formations in Hang Va range from a few centime to over a meter in height. The water in the pools is perfectly clear. In photographs lit by expedition lamps, the reflection of the cave ceiling in the pool surfaces creates an illusion of infinite depth, as if each pool is a window into another cave below. The cave is not open to mass tourism. According to the Fong Naang National Park Administration, access is restricted to guided expeditions limited to small groups. The Cowsite terraces are fragile. A single footstep on a rimstone dam can destroy a formation that took 10,000 years to build. A cave with a floor that looks like a flooded rice patty built by water and chemistry over millennia, one molecular layer at a time. No human designed it. No human could. And the only way to see it without destroying it is to look and not touch, which for most of human history has been the one thing we are worst at. Number seven, Leugia Cave. Carl'sbad, New Mexico, USA. In 1986, a group of cavers in Carl'sbad Caverns National Park noticed something unusual about a small, unremarkable pit in the desert that had been known for decades, but never seriously explored. Air was blowing out of it. Strong, consistent air flow, the kind that indicates a large passage system behind a blockage. They dug through the rubble at the bottom. What they broke into was one of the most scientifically significant cave systems ever discovered. According to the US National Park Service, Lechugia Cave extends over 240 km of mapped passage, making it one of the longest caves in the United States. Its depth reaches roughly 489 m. The cave contains formations of a type and scale found almost nowhere else. Massive gypsum chandeliers hanging from ceilings, hydromagnusite balloon formations that look like inflated white soap bubbles, and pools of water so still and so clear that explorers have accidentally stepped into them, mistaking the surface for dry rock. But the discovery that made Lechugia internationally significant had nothing to do with geology. In 2012, a research team led by microbiologist Hazel Barton of the University of Akran published a study in the journal Plus 1 that changed how scientists think about antibiotic resistance. Barton's team collected bacteria from deep within Lechugia, organisms living on bare rock in total darkness, sealed off from the surface for an estimated 4 to 7 million years. These bacteria had never encountered a human antibiotic. They had never been exposed to pharmaceutical compounds of any kind. When the researchers tested the bacteria against a panel of modern clinical antibiotics, the bacteria were resistant to multiple drugs. Drugs that pharmaceutical companies had developed within the last few decades. According to Barton's published analysis, the resistance mechanisms in the cave bacteria were functionally similar to those found in hospital superbugs. The implication was profound. Antibiotic resistance is not a modern problem created by the overuse of medicine. It is an ancient biological strategy, millions of years old, developed by bacteria competing for survival in environments where other microbes produce natural antibiotic compounds. Lechugia is now one of the most protected caves on Earth. Access requires a research permit approved by the National Park Service. Fewer than 100 people have ever entered the deep sections. Cavers are required to decontaminate all equipment and clothing before entry to prevent introducing surface organisms that could contaminate the cave's pristine microbial ecosystem. A cave that was ignored for decades because it looked like nothing. A blast of air through rubble and behind it 240 km of passage containing organisms that had been quietly evolving resistance to drugs that humans would not invent for another 4 million years. Number six, Postonia Cave. Postonia, Slovenia. Roughly 50 km southwest of Ljubljana, a cave system has been open to tourists since 1819. Over 39 million people have visited. A railway was installed in 1872, one of the oldest underground railways on Earth. Visitors ride a small train through illuminated passages of stellagtites and stelagmmites for roughly 3.7 km before disembarking and walking through the remaining sections on foot. None of that is what makes Postonia remarkable. What makes Postonia remarkable lives in the water. The m proteius and is a caved dwelling amphibian found only in the subterranean rivers and lakes of the daeneric karst a limestone region stretching across Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia. According to research published by the department of biology at the University of Ljubljana, the M is the largest cave adapted animal in Europe. It is completely blind. It has no pigmentation. Its skin is pale, translucent, almost pink. It breathes through external gills that protrude from its head like feathered antenna and it lives for over a hundred years. According to a 2010 study published in the journal Biology Letters by ecologist Yan Voyteran of the University of Leon, the M has an estimated maximum lifespan exceeding 100 years. Extraordinary for an amphibian of its size. For comparison, a similarly sized salamander on the surface lives roughly 10 to 15 years. The M's metabolism is so slow that according to Voyter's research, it can survive without food for up to 10 years. Not hibernate, survive, active and moving, metabolizing stored reserves at a rate that science struggles to explain. In 2016, an M in Postoia cave laid eggs. The first time reproduction had been observed in captivity. According to the Posonia cave management team, which live streamed the event, the eggs took 120 days to develop, the first baby emerged in June 2016. It was roughly 2 cm long, translucent, blind from birth, born into permanent darkness, the only world its species has known for an estimated 20 million years. The M was first described in 1689 by Slovenian naturalist Yanz Vikard Valvasaur, who reported that local people believed the creatures were baby dragons washed out of underground layers by floods. According to Valvasaur's account, preserved in his encyclopedic work, the glory of the duche of Carniola, the appearance of Ms in surface streams after heavy rains convinced local communities that dragons lived in the caves. An animal that lives for a century without seeing light, that survives a decade without eating, that was mistaken for a baby dragon for hundreds of years, and that has been evolving in the dark rivers beneath Slovenia since before the human species existed. If you are still watching, you already know this channel is for you. Hit subscribe and tell us in the comments which cave has been the most unsettling so far. The top five go deeper. Number five, Cave of the Crystals, Nika, Chihuahua, Mexico. 300 meters beneath the Sierra Dika in northern Mexico, inside an active lead and silver mine, there is a chamber that was sealed from the outside world for roughly 500,000 years. In April 2000, miners drilling a new tunnel broke through a wall and found it. Inside the chamber, crystals, selonite crystals, the largest natural crystals ever found on Earth. According to geological analysis led by Dr. Juan Manuel Garcia Ruiz of the University of Granada, published in the journal Geology, the crystals in the cave of the crystals are composed of gypsum in its transparent selonite form. The largest measured crystal is 12 m long, roughly 4 m wide, and weighs an estimated 55 tons. For scale, that is taller than a four-story building. And it grew, not was placed, not was carved, grew molecule by molecule over approximately 500,000 years. According to Garcia Ruiz's research, the crystals formed in a narrow temperature window. The cave was flooded with minerals saturated water heated by a magma chamber. below. At temperatures between 54 and 58° C, the dissolved minerals precipitated out of solution at a rate slow enough to produce enormous defect-free crystals. The process was measured in micrometers per century. The chamber is lethal to unprotected humans. The air temperature is 58° C, roughly 136 F. Humidity is between 90 and 99%. According to research published by the Italian National Institute of Geoysics and Volcanology, a human being without specialized cooling equipment loses the ability to regulate body temperature within approximately 10 minutes of entering the cave. Sweat cannot evaporate in air that is already saturated. Core body temperature rises rapidly. Confusion sets in. Unconsciousness follows. Researchers who entered the cave wore refrigerated suits filled with ice and carried oxygen supplies. Even with protection, exploration was limited to sessions of roughly 30 to 45 minutes. According to the mine operators, industrias penles, the pumps that kept the cave drained were shut down in 2015 due to operational costs. The cave has reflooded. The crystals are once again submerged in the hot mineral water that created them. They are still growing right now in the dark at a rate too slow for any human lifespan to observe. A chamber sealed for half a million years. Crystals taller than houses built one molecule at a time. An environment so hostile that humans can survive 10 minutes inside. And now it is sealed again, flooded, dark, and adding another layer so thin it will not be measurable for another century. Number four, Cistma Sak Actun, Kintanaroo, Mexico. Beneath the jungle floor of the Yucatan Peninsula, there is a flooded cave system that stretches over 370 km of mapped underwater passage. According to the Kintanaroo Speliological Survey, Systemma Sak Octon is the longest known underwater cave system on Earth. The system has no single entrance. Hundreds of cenotes, circular sinkholes in the limestone, provide access points scattered across the jungle. Each cenote is a window into the same vast underground river network that connects them all. The caves were above water during the last ice age when sea levels were roughly 120 m lower than today. According to archaeological research published by the National Institute of Anthropology and History of Mexico, humans lived in them. They walked on dry floors, lit fires, and left behind objects that have been sitting in the dark for over 12,000 years. When the ice melted and the seas rose, the caves flooded. The fresh water that filled them preserved what was inside. Divers have found the skeletal remains of humans dating back over 13,000 years. Some of the oldest human remains in the Americas. According to research published in the journal POS1 by a team from the National Autonomous University of Mexico, the skeleton known as NIA discovered in the submerged pit called Hoyo Negro at a depth of over 40 m was a teenage girl who fell into the cave roughly 12,000 to 13,000 years ago. DNA analysis confirmed her as genetically related to modern indigenous populations of the Americas. But the human remains are not alone. The caves contain the bones of megapaa, giant ground sloths, saber-tooththed cats, gulthears, and other ice age animals that entered the caves when they were dry and never left. According to paleontological surveys published by the institut national dean anthropologia aistoria the underwater passages function as a time capsule of the pleaene a preserved snapshot of the ecosystem that existed in the yucatan before the water came. Cave diving in the cenotes is among the most dangerous forms of diving in the world. According to the international association for cave diving hundreds of divers have died in the yucatan cenote systems. The primary risks are disorientation in zero visibility conditions when silt is disturbed, loss of contact with the guideline, and the distance to the nearest air source when something goes wrong. 370 km of mapped passage, unmapped kilm beyond that. The bones of a 13,000year-old girl resting on a cave floor next to the skeleton of a saber-tooththed cat. Both of them walked in on dry ground and the ocean rose behind them and sealed the entrance for 10,000 years. Number three, Krera Veronia Cave. Arabica Massie, Western Caucuses, Georgia. In the mountains of the Western Caucuses near the coast of the Black Sea in the disputed territory of Abcasia, there is a cave entrance at 2,256 m above sea level that looks like nothing. a crack in the limestone, a dark gap between rocks on a windswept alpine plateau. Below that crack, the earth drops for over two kilometers. Kbera Veronia was first explored in the 1960s by Soviet speliologists who reached a depth of roughly 340 m before a sump, a passage completely filled with water, stopped them. According to records from the Ukrainian speliological association, the cave was largely abandoned for decades. Other systems in the region seemed more promising. In 2001, a Ukrainian expedition led by Yuri Kazjan returned. They pushed past the sump that had stopped the Soviets. Behind it, the cave continued and continued and continued. Over the following years, successive expeditions pushed deeper. Each one required camps underground, not quick descents and returns, but multi-day expeditions where teams lived inside the cave for a week or more at a time. According to expedition reports published by the Ukrainian Spelological Association, the deeper camps were established at roughly 700 m, 1,200 m, and 1,600 m below the surface. Supplies were carried down by hand through vertical shafts, tight squeezes, and waterfalls of ice cold meltwater. In 2004, an expedition reached 2,80 m. In 2007, another team pushed to 2,191 m. In 2012, a Ukrainian diver named Gennady Samoken pushed through a terminal sump at the bottom and reached 2,197 m, the deepest point any human had reached inside the Earth. Kbera held the record for the deepest cave in the world for over a decade. The conditions at depth were extreme. According to expedition physician Dr. Yenni Snetkcov whose medical reports were published by the Ukrainian Speliological Association. Cavers at the deepest camps experienced elevated heart rates, disrupted sleep cycles and psychological effects from prolonged total darkness and confinement. The temperature at depth is a constant 3 to 7° C. The humidity is 100%. Everything is wet. Nothing dries. The sound at the bottom of Kera is water. The cave is fed by snowmelt from the Arabica massif above. The water descends through the system and emerges at a spring near the Black Sea coast, a journey that researchers have confirmed using dieaccing studies published by the Georgian Institute of Hydrogeeology. The distance the water travels from the cave entrance to the coastal spring is roughly 13 km horizontally and over 2,000 m vertically, a crack in a mountain side, 2 km straight down. camps at depths where the sun has not reached in geological epochs. And at the bottom, water flowing through passages that no human has followed toward an ocean that most of the cavers above will never see from this angle. But Kera is no longer the deepest. That record was taken and the cave that took it is only 15 km away. Number two, Qua de los Taios, Morona, Santiago Province, Ecuador. In the dense jungle of southeastern Ecuador on the eastern slopes of the Andes, there is a cave system that descends roughly 200 m into the rock beneath the Coangos River Valley. By the standards of this list, 200 m is not deep. Krera is 10 times deeper. Varovkina is 11 times deeper. Qua Dillos Taios is not on this list because of its depth. It is on this list because of who went inside and why. In July 1976, an expedition entered the cave. It was not a small team. According to records from the British Army's Royal Engineers, who provided logistical support, the expedition included over a 100 participants, military personnel, scientists, cavers, and documentary filmmakers. It was funded by the government of Ecuador, supported by the British military, and covered by international press. The expedition leader was Stan Hall, a Scottish engineer. The most prominent member was Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on the moon 7 years after Apollo 11, descended into a cave in the Ecuadorian jungle. Armstrong's participation was not casual. According to Hall's expedition records, later compiled in his book Taios Gold, Armstrong served as the honorary expedition leader, and spent several days inside the cave, descending through the main shaft and exploring the lower chambers. The question that everyone asked then and still asks now is why? Why would the first man on the moon go into a cave in Ecuador? The answer traces back to a book published in 1973 by Eric Vonanakin, the Swiss author of Chariots of the Gods. Vanakin claimed that a Hungarian Argentine explorer named Yanos Juan Morates had discovered a vast underground library inside Qua Dillos Taios in 1969. A library containing metallic tablets inscribed with an unknown writing system left by an advanced prehistoric civilization. According to Von Danakin's account, Morics reported the discovery to the Ecuadorian government, but refused to reveal the exact location within the cave system. The 1976 expedition was in part an attempt to verify these claims. The expedition spent weeks inside the cave. They mapped passages. They collected geological and biological samples. They documented the cave's extraordinary population of oil birds, the Teaos, from which the cave takes its name. Large nocturnal birds that navigate by echolocation, one of the few bird species on Earth to do so. According to ornithological records published by the expedition, the bird's clicks echoed through the chambers in a constant stream of sound. The metallic library was not found. According to the expedition's official scientific reports, no artifacts of artificial manufacture were discovered within the cave system. The chambers were natural limestone formations. The walls were bare rock. Armstrong never publicly explained his full motivation for participating. In interviews collected by Hall and preserved in the expedition archive, Armstrong described the cave as impressive and said the experience of descending into the earth reminded him in a different way of the experience of leaving it. The Schwar people, the indigenous inhabitants of the region consider the cave sacred. According to ethnographic research by anthropologist Father Juan Botaso of the Celisian Mission, the Schwar have entered the cave for centuries to collect oilbird chicks, a valued food source during specific seasons governed by traditional law. The cave in Schwar cosmology is an entrance to the world beneath the world, a place where the spirits of ancestors reside. A cave in the jungle, a library that was never found. the first man on the moon climbing down into the earth 7 years after he walked on its satellite. Oil birds navigating by sound in the dark. And a people who have always known the cave was significant not because of metal tablets but because of what they believe lives in the silence below the birds. Number one, Viokina cave Arabica massif Cauasus, Georgia. 15 km from the entrance of Kubera on the same windswept limestone plateau of the Arabica Massie at 2,39 m above sea level there is another crack in the rock another dark gap that looks like nothing from the surface. Below it lies the deepest known point inside the earth that any human being has ever reached. Varovkina cave was first explored in 1968 by a Georgian speliological team. They descended roughly 115 m and stopped at a constriction too tight to pass. According to records from the Perovo Speliological Club of Moscow, the cave was revisited periodically over the following decades, but progress was slow. The upper sections of the cave are a maze of tight vertical shafts connected by passages that require technical rope work and in several places the removal of rock to widen openings enough for a human body to pass. Serious exploration resumed in the 2000s. Russian expeditions from the Perovo Club pushed deeper yearbyear. In 2015, they reached 1,832 m. In 2016, 2,24 m. And in March 2018, a team of five Russian cavers reached 2,212 m below the entrance, surpassing Kbera's record of 2,197 m and establishing Variokina as the deepest cave on Earth. The 2018 expedition lasted roughly 1 month. According to the detailed expedition report published by the Perovo Spelological Club, the team established a series of underground camps connected by fixed ropes. The descent from camp to camp required navigating vertical drops of up to 200 m, tight meanders where the passage width narrowed to less than 40 cm, and multiple waterfalls of glacial meltwater pouring through the shafts. At certain depths, the waterfall shafts are inescapable. The cavers descended through the falling water itself. Ropes soaked, equipment drenched, bodies losing heat with every meter. According to the expedition physician, several team members exhibited early symptoms of hypothermia at the deeper camps despite wearing multiple layers and sleeping in bivoax sacks designed for extreme cold. The temperature at depth is a constant 4 to 6° C. Combined with 100% humidity and no possibility of drying equipment, the cold becomes cumulative. The deepest point reached 2,212 m. Below the surface, was not a chamber or a flat surface. It was a sump, a passage completely filled with water. The cavers could see the tunnel continuing beyond the water. The passage did not end, but without diving equipment rated for the depth and conditions, equipment that would need to be carried over 2 km down through the cave system described above, the exploration stopped. According to the expedition report, the team spent roughly 3 hours at the deepest point before beginning the ascent. The return to the surface took 5 days. Each camp was dismantled. Equipment was hauled upward through the same shafts and waterfalls and the team emerged into daylight having spent a month underground. What was found at the bottom of Verovkina has raised questions that remain unanswered. According to hydrogeeological analysis published by the Georgian Institute of Earth Sciences, dieracing experiments have confirmed that water entering Verofkina's upper shafts eventually emerges at springs near the Black Sea coast. a horizontal distance of roughly 13 kilometers and a vertical distance of over 2,000 meters. The underground river system that connects the cave bottom to the sea has never been mapped. The passages through which the water travels are too small, too flooded, or too dangerous for human exploration. But the most significant discovery was biological. According to a 2019 study published in the journal Subterranean Biology by researchers from the Russian Academy of Sciences, a new species of invertebrate was identified at a depth of approximately 2,000 m inside Verofkina. A tiny eyeless creature adapted to permanent darkness. Found clinging to rock surfaces in the deepest sections of the cave. It was named Plutomerous Ortobalaganis. It is the deepest dwelling terrestrial organism ever discovered. An animal with no eyes living on bare rock 2 km beneath the surface of the earth in a place where no light has reached since before the human species evolved. It has been there longer than us. It will likely be thereafter. Varovkina is not finished. The sump at 2,212 m is not the end of the cave. It is the end of what humans have been able to reach. The passage continues beyond the water. The river continues flowing. The rock continues descending. Every speliologist who has studied the Arabica Massie agrees on one thing. According to geological surveys published by the Georgian Academy of Sciences, the theoretical maximum depth of the cave systems in the Massie could exceed 2,700 m based on the elevation of the plateau and the known depth of the coastal springs where the water emerges. 500 m of cave that no one has seen. Passages that exist right now in the darkness beneath a mountain in the western Caucasus, carrying water from the alpine snow to the Black Sea through a route that no map has ever recorded. A crack in a plateau 2 km down, a month underground, an eyeless animal on a rock in the deepest dark on Earth, a river at the bottom flowing toward an ocean. And beyond the last point any human has reached, the cave keeps going. Nobody knows how far. 10 caves. A mountain in Austria filled with ice that has been building for centuries. A hole in Mexico where tens of thousands of birds spiral out at dawn and dive back in at dusk. A chamber in Vietnam with a floor that looks like flooded rice patties made of stone. A cave in New Mexico where bacteria developed resistance to drugs that would not be invented for 4 million years. A blind animal in Slovenia that lives for a century and eats once a decade. A sealed chamber in Mexico with crystals taller than houses in air that kills in 10 minutes. 370 km of flooded tunnel in the Yucatan with 13,000year-old bones on the floor. A 2 km descent in the Caucasus through waterfalls and darkness. A cave in Ecuador where the first man on the moon searched for a library that was never found. And the deepest point on Earth that any human has ever reached, 2,212 m down, with the cave still going beyond the water. We have mapped the surface of Mars in higher resolution than we have mapped what is beneath our own feet. The deepest ocean trench has been visited by more people than the bottom of Verovkina. And every cave on this list was found the same way. Someone noticed a crack, felt a breeze, and decided to see where it went. The Earth is not solid. It is full of holes. And most of those holes have never been entered, never lit, never measured, never named. They exist right now in the dark beneath mountains and deserts and cities and oceans, holding water and bones and crystals and creatures that have never seen the sun.
